item.description:
UAE-funded mercenary targeted British activist in London, report says

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 08/19/2026 - 20:05
UAE allegedly funded an operation to surveil British-Muslim activist Anas al-Tikriti, with a US mercenary reportedly discussing the possibility of killing him, ITV News reports
Anas al-Tikriti told ITV News that he felt physically sick after being shown messages and photographs gathered by Abraham Golan (Screengrab/X)
Off

A mercenary allegedly hired and paid millions of dollars by the United Arab Emirates carried out a covert surveillance operation against a British activist and academic in London, according to an investigation by ITV News.

Abraham Golan, a dual Hungarian-Israeli citizen who ran the private security company Spear Operations Group, travelled to Britain in December 2016 to target Anas al-Tikriti, the chief executive of the London-based Cordoba Foundation think tank, ITV News reported on Wednesday.

Emirati financial records seen by ITV showed that Golan, who lived in the US, was being paid by the UAE while carrying out the operation. He was receiving a six-figure annual retainer, as well as substantial bonuses, including a $1m payment weeks before his trip to London for an operation in Yemen.

ITV's investigation, based on witness testimony, emails, WhatsApp messages and financial records, found that Golan worked with a former US special forces operative to locate and monitor Tikriti.

According to the UK broadcaster, Golan told a British strategist assisting him that he was working for the UAE and that Abu Dhabi considered Tikriti and the Cordoba Foundation to be aligned with groups it regarded as terrorist organisations.

Golan contacted the British strategist, identified by ITV as "Victor", in November 2016, asking whether he had any "channels" to Tikriti and the Cordoba Foundation.

According to the report, Golan later travelled to London, where he offered Victor £50,000 ($68,000) to help locate Tikriti, increasing the offer to £100,000 ($136,000).

Golan shared photographs of Tikriti's home and car, maps and satellite images, and details of his movements between home and work.

At one meeting, Golan allegedly discussed the possibility of physically eliminating Tikriti. His associate, a former US Navy Seal, reportedly made a gesture across his throat when asked what could happen to the activist.

"I became increasingly worried about what this operation entailed," Victor told ITV.

Britain must reject the UAE's Brotherhood bogeyman
Read More »

In a follow-up message, Golan appeared to suggest that the operation was part of a much wider campaign. "War is coming to Europe and we are at the beginning of a huge program," he wrote to Victor, without elaborating on what he meant.

Golan subsequently left the UK for Washington but told Victor that the operation would continue, writing that his "team" remained in London.

Victor eventually withdrew from the operation after concluding it could involve an assassination.

The extent to which the surveillance continued is unclear. Tikriti, who has helped negotiate the release of more than 20 hostages across Africa and the Middle East, was later visited twice at his London home by police officers who warned him that his life could be at risk.

The officers did not tell him the source or nature of the threat.

"I feel physically sick," Tikriti told ITV News after being shown the messages and photographs gathered by Golan.

"At the time, my children were three and one and a half years old," he said.

UAE's Muslim Brotherhood campaign

The alleged operation came amid a long-running dispute between the UAE and the UK over the Muslim Brotherhood.

For years, the UAE has accused the Muslim Brotherhood of threatening its political system and has sought to suppress the movement and its influence across the region since the Arab Spring.

Founded in Cairo in 1928, the Muslim Brotherhood is one of the world's largest and best-known political Islam groups. 

It has long maintained that it is a peaceful organisation that wishes to participate in politics democratically, but it is considered a major threat by several autocratic governments in the region.

In 2014, Abu Dhabi designated the Cordoba Foundation, the Muslim Association of Britain, and Islamic Relief as terrorist organisations alongside groups including the Islamic State group (IS) and al-Qaeda.

What is driving Britain's Muslim Brotherhood panic?
Read More »

However, a year later, in 2015, a UK government review found no evidence that the Muslim Brotherhood was involved in terrorist activity in Britain.

The Cordoba Foundation has consistently denied having a formal association with the Muslim Brotherhood.

Tikriti has acknowledged studying the group's ideology but rejected suggestions that he poses a threat.

"I'm a Brit. I grew up in Britain," he told ITV News. "In my life, I have never done anything wrong whatsoever."

According to ITV News, Golan's alleged operation in London also followed his work for the UAE in Yemen.

In 2015, his company was hired to assemble a team of western military veterans to target people Abu Dhabi considered linked to the Muslim Brotherhood. 

One of the targets was Yemeni MP Anssaf Ali Mayo, whose office was targeted with explosives. 

Mayo has since said he suffers "psychological and emotional trauma" from the assassination attempt, and now lives in exile in Saudi Arabia. His wife and two children remain in Yemen. 

Golan later acknowledged the existence of a "targeted assassination" programme in Yemen, telling BuzzFeed News that it had been "sanctioned" by the UAE.

A former member of his team, US Special Forces veteran Dale Comstock, told ITV News: "For all intents and purposes, we were Emirati soldiers."

According to ITV News, the London operation took place as Britain and the UAE were publicly deepening their political and economic relationship.

Two weeks after Golan first contacted Victor, then Prince Charles travelled to Abu Dhabi to strengthen bilateral ties.

British officials were aware of disagreements with the UAE over the Muslim Brotherhood, but said they had no knowledge that a covert operation involving mercenaries was being planned on the UK's shores.

A Home Office spokesperson told ITV: "It is our longstanding policy not to comment on security and intelligence matters."

MEE contacted the UAE's embassies in Britain and the US for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

Oil supertankers in Gulf are renting for $500,000 per day: Report

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 08/19/2026 - 21:10
A fund that allows investors to bet on crude oil freight rates has surged more than 2,000 percent since the start of year
In this picture, obtained from Iran's ISNA news agency and taken on 2 May 2026, the Gambia-flagged tanker Bili is anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas in southern Iran (Amirhossein Khorgooei/ISNA/AFP)
Off

Supertanker owners are getting paid $510,000 per day to bring crude oil from the Gulf to Asia, in a sign of high demand for vessels to transit the waterway as fighting rages in the region and alternative routes take supply from the market.

Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that earnings from the Middle East-to-China route have jumped to their highest level since June.

The rising figure suggests that demand for vessels is high and some are risking the threat of war to take profits. 

“Right now, the strait is open. A lot of boats are coming through. People aren’t reporting that," US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday. 

One vessel, a very large crude carrier (VLCC), the Mongolia Prosperity, operated by South Korean shipowner Sinokor, is set to load crude from an unnamed Persian Gulf port for delivery to East Asia, with the voyage costing $31m, Bloomberg reported.

A ceasefire struck in April amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, and extended in June, is all but defunct in the Strait of Hormuz, with each side trying to impose its own blockade.

The US military fired on a Panama-flagged container ship earlier this month that it said attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman to an Iranian port.

Meanwhile, at least one sailor was killed this week in Iranian attacks on vessels transiting the water, the Joint Maritime Information Centre, a multinational organisation, said.

But Gulf states are still trying to export millions of barrels of oil to customers in Asia. 

UAE's Adnoc announces $8bn gas expansion, as it mulls Hormuz bypass
Read More »

The fighting means that shipowners willing to brave the risk stand to make handsome profits with demand high and the supply of vessels low.

The Breakwave Tanker Shipping ETF (BWET), which allows investors to bet on the price of crude oil freight futures, is up a whopping 2,200 percent since the start of the year. BWET surged after the US and Israel attacked Iran in April, then fell when the ceasefire was declared. But it has soared in value over the summer as investors bet against an end to fighting in Hormuz. 

Yemen’s Houthis have restarted attacking vessels in the Red Sea. To avoid the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint, Saudi Arabia has had to send oil via the Sumed Pipeline to the Mediterranean, where it is loaded onto VLCC tankers. The vessels take a longer route around the tip of Africa, reducing the supply of ships available in the market and driving up prices.

The Trump administration has insisted that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that more vessels are transiting the waterway than is being publicly reported. 

The UAE boosted oil production to an all-time high in June, pumping 4.1 million barrels per day, the International Energy Agency said in a July report. The UAE has taken a risk-prone approach to sending vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, with its ship-tracking signals turned off.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] US elections: Progressive Democrat scores shock win in Florida
item.description:
US elections: Progressive Democrat scores shock win in Florida

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 08/19/2026 - 21:22
Voters delivered a mixed bag for US President Donald Trump's allies in Republican primaries
Democratic US Senate candidate, Florida state Representative Angie Nixon, participates in a worship service during a visit to the Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church, on 17 August 2026, in Hallandale Beach, Florida (Joe Raedle/ Getty Images North America via AFP)
Off

Voters headed to the polls in three US states on Tuesday for a series of Democratic and Republican primaries. 

The verdict in Alaska, Florida, and Wyoming testified to a Democratic Party split along establishment lines and progressives critical of US support for Israel and the war on Iran. 

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) played a key role in several races. 

Aipac showered funds on candidates on both sides of the aisle to defeat opponents critical of the US's interventions in the Middle East. 

Meanwhile, some challengers sought to tie voters' concerns about the cost of living to the cost of the US-Israeli war on Iran. 

Overall, the results underscored the establishment's hold on the states. 

Florida: Progressive Democrat has surprise win

In Florida, State Representative Angie Nixon, a Democratic Socialist and former union organiser, defeated Alexander Vindman, a retired army lieutenant colonel and national security council aide, in the Democratic primary race for governor. 

The margin and the financial disparity were formidable, as Nixon raised less than $1m, while Vindman raised more than $16m. Nixon's campaign emphasised an anti-war stance alongside Medicare for All and affordable housing. 

On the Republican side, Congressman Bryon Donalds won the primary against a field of candidates.

Donalds was endorsed by US President Donald Trump and came under intense criticism from challenger James Fishback for his closeness to Aipac. Fishback, who was endorsed by far-right podcaster Nick Fuentes, campaigned critically against US support for Israel and the war on Iran. He was also endorsed by podcaster Tucker Carlson. 

Florida has become a solidly red state in recent elections, and Donalds is widely expected to win the November general election and succeed Governor Ron DeSantis.

Trump-backed Congressman Cory Mills lost his Florida primary after months of controversy and a House Ethics Committee investigation involving allegations of campaign finance violations and sexual misconduct.

Alaska and Wyoming: Aipac candidates unchallenged 

Alaska’s primaries cemented the hold of establishment parties endorsed by Aipac on both sides of the aisle.

Former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola and Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan both advanced in the state’s nonpartisan Senate primary. 

Peltola’s campaign focused on Alaskan fisheries and the energy sector. She received more than $96,546 from Aipac and limited her criticism of the US war on Iran to the issue of more stringent congressional oversight. 

Wyoming offered little evidence of a Democratic reckoning.

Republicans maintained their dominance of the state, nominating Harriet Hageman for the Senate seat being vacated by Senator Cynthia Lummis and Chuck Gray for Hageman’s House seat. 

Hageman is an ally of Trump and has vocally supported the US war on Iran and military aid for Israel.

item.description:
UK condemns Israel's E1 settlement expansion in occupied West Bank

Britain's foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has criticised Israel's move this week to launch a construction tender for the E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank as an "unacceptable and destructive act". 

Miliband indicated that he made it clear to the Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa'ar that the "Israeli Government must halt E1 plans immediately, retract the tender and stop all settlement expansion".

"The impact of settler violence and terrorism has been catastrophic for Palestinian communities. Settlement expansion and attempts to create irreversible divisions on the ground threaten peace, security and the prospects for a viable Palestinian state," he said. 

Miliband expressed that the UK will not "stand back and accept the destruction" of the two-state solution, adding that the country is "will set out a comprehensive set of measures" in the coming weeks, including sanctions targeting those involved in illegal settlement expansion.

UK Minister of State for the Middle East Stephen Doughty has also joined Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in condemning Israel, describing the move as a "deliberate and destructive act designed to undermine a two-state solution".
